title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief analysis of Robbie Andrew's (CICERO) extraction-based CO2 dataset shows Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are history's largest CO2 exporters; counting exports quadruples Saudi Arabia's and doubles Australia's historical emissions, while import-reliant Japan, Germany and others fall in the rankings and the US and China stay on top.

insights.claim: Carbon Brief analysis of extraction-based accounting finds Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the largest exporters of CO2 in history, measured by emissions from fossil fuels they exported and that were burned abroad since 1850.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Producer-based responsibility framing targets major hydrocarbon exporters, raising reputational and policy pressure on their export volumes.
insights.quote: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history
insights.locator: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president

insights.claim: Other major historical CO2 exporters via overseas fossil-fuel sales since 1850 include Venezuela, Iran, Norway, the UAE and Canada, which together with the top three have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 over 175 years.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Identifies the set of petrostates most exposed if supply-side or extraction-based climate accountability gains traction.
insights.locator: Other major CO2 exporters, based on

insights.claim: Including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports more than doubles Australia's share of historical warming and lifts it into the top ten historical emitters.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Australia's coal and LNG export model is increasingly a diplomatic liability, especially while it co-presides over COP31.
insights.locator: Australia also climbs up the rankings

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's cumulative CO2 emissions rise more than fourfold under extraction-based accounting, making it responsible for the world's fifth-largest share of historical warming.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Strengthens the case used by climate negotiators to push oil exporters toward greater finance or phase-down commitments.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia becomes responsible for the

insights.claim: Russia stays third among historical emitters under extraction-based accounting despite gaining responsibility for an extra 69bn tonnes of CO2 from exported fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Quantifies Russia's hydrocarbon-export footprint, relevant to sanctions and fossil-trade debates.

insights.claim: The US and China retain the largest responsibility for historical warming even under extraction-based accounting, despite both being net CO2 importers since 1850.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Accounting method changes the ordering below the top two but not the US/China dominance in cumulative emissions.

insights.claim: The US was a major oil importer until the shale revolution in the early 2000s, while China remains a major oil and gas importer, describing itself as rich in coal but lacking oil and gas.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Import dependence shapes how energy importers frame climate responsibility and energy security policy.
insights.quote: rich in coal, lacking oil and gas

insights.claim: The UK becomes the fourth-largest historical emitter under extraction-based accounting, overtaking Germany, which falls because of its reliance on fossil-fuel imports.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: North Sea extraction history adds to the UK's climate-responsibility exposure relative to import-dependent peers.

insights.claim: Japan, almost completely reliant on fossil-fuel imports, ranks as the sixth-largest historical emitter on a territorial basis but only 34th on an extraction basis; Germany, India, France and Turkey also fall under extraction accounting.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Import-dependent economies have an incentive to champion producer-side accountability in climate negotiations.
insights.locator: Japan is a particularly notable example

insights.claim: On a per-capita basis, small oil and gas exporting nations such as Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar, Norway and Trinidad and Tobago have the highest extraction-based CO2 emissions since 1850.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Small hydrocarbon-dependent economies are the most exposed per head to supply-side climate accountability arguments.
insights.locator: Small nations that export large amounts

insights.claim: Historical climate responsibility can be allocated by territorial emissions, consumption of imported goods, colonial rule, per-capita emissions, or extraction location, and the extraction lens shifts the spotlight onto major fossil-fuel exporters.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Which accounting frame wins in negotiations determines which countries face pressure for finance and phase-down.

insights.claim: CICERO researcher Robbie Andrew, whose draft 1850-2025 dataset underpins the analysis, argues that responsibility for burning fossil fuels is shared jointly between extractors, producers and consumers, noting Middle East oil was historically developed for western powers.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Signals extraction-based accounting is unlikely to be adopted as a sole basis for liability; expect hybrid framings.
insights.quote: it’s joint responsibility between extractors, producers and consumers

insights.claim: Australia faces pressure for continuing to expand fossil-fuel production while serving as co-president of the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya alongside host Turkey.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Watch for COP31 outcomes or Australian policy moves touching new coal and gas project approvals.

insights.claim: This year is expected to be around 1.5C above pre-industrial temperatures and next year is forecast to be the hottest on record at around 1.7C of warming, with approximately 100% of warming to date attributed to human greenhouse gas emissions.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Record temperatures sustain political momentum behind climate policy and fossil-fuel scrutiny.
